title: Built a deterministic 2D tactical artillery game in Godot 4.7 using an AI-assisted asset & code pipeline (Playable in browser on itch.io)
author: Belsaga
selftext:
I've been working on Bug Wars: Tactical Backyard, a 2D turn-based tactical artillery game (Worms-style) built in Godot 4.7 with destructible pixel terrain, 3 asymmetric insect factions, surface chemistry (acid, sticky sap, silk bridges), and deterministic 1v1 online multiplayer. I just put a playable WebGL build up on [itch.io](http://itch.io) here: [https://belsaga.itch.io/bug-wars](https://belsaga.itch.io/bug-wars) 

Since this community focuses on the actual AI dev process rather than just dropping a trailer, I wanted to share the workflow I ended up with—specifically where AI saved me weeks of work and where it kept breaking things until I built strict guardrails around it.

For art and audio, generating assets one by one in web UIs quickly became a bottleneck, especially for consistency. Instead, I wrote a batch pipeline in Python using Replicate and PixelLab for faction cards, weapon icons, backgrounds, and explosions, plus ElevenLabs and Kokoro-ONNX for faction voice lines and music. Even then, raw AI outputs weren't drop-in ready: I still had to write post-processing scripts for sprite slicing, readability/palette cleanup, seamless audio looping, and a Godot script (bake\_normals.gd) to generate normal maps so the 2D lighting actually worked on weapons and terrain.

On the code side, I used coding agents hooked up to a Godot MCP (godot-ai) to iterate on GDScript systems and run headless simulations. It was great for scaffolding UI, modular .tres faction/weapon resources, and tooling, but AI agents really struggled with deterministic lockstep multiplayer. Whenever an agent introduced a casual randf() or frame-dependent timing into gameplay or procedural map code, online matches would desync immediately.

To stop AI-generated changes from silently breaking determinism, I had to build a fairly strict safety net: isolated SplitMix64 RNG streams so decorative foliage never affects terrain collision, a MapValidator that rejects or auto-repairs bad procedural maps, and a headless determinism\_gate.py test that runs fixed-60-FPS simulations and fails the build if two runs with the same seed ever diverge.

If you try the browser build on [itch.io](http://itch.io), I'd really appreciate feedback on how the game feels to play—and I'm curious how others here handle consistency and automated QA when letting AI touch core gameplay systems.
